We estimated 5-year mortality risk, risk differences (RDs), and multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs for the association between comorbid dementia and cancer-specific and all-cause mortality, overall and across key patient and cancer characteristics. FINDINGS: We identified 17 425 patients with cancer and comorbid dementia and 86 823 patients with cancer without comorbid dementia. Patients with cancer and comorbid dementia had a 5-year cancer-specific mortality of 44·0% (95% CI 43·2-44·7) compared with 39·4% (39·1-39·8) among patients with cancer without comorbid dementia (RD 4·5%, 95% CI 3·7-5·4), and an excess 5-year all-cause mortality (22·2%, 21·5-22·9). Excess cancer-specific mortality associated with dementia was the highest among patients with colon cancer (RD 13·8%, 95% CI 10·8-16·7), rectal cancer (RD 14·8%, 95% CI 10.3-19.2), and breast cancer (RD 8·9%, 95% CI 6·3-11·5%). Comparison of patients with cancer and comorbid dementia with patients those with cancer alone revealed higher cancer-specific mortality (multivariable-adjusted HR 1·28, 95% CI 1·24-1·31) and all-cause mortality (2·03, 1·98-2·07) among patients with cancer and dementia. INTERPRETATION: Cancer-specific and all-cause mortality rates were elevated among individuals with cancer and dementia. As treatments continue to improve survival outcomes for people with cancer and dementia, clinical guidelines for cancer screening and treatment in individuals living with dementia should be developed. FUNDING: National Institutes of Health, Aarhus University.

title: RSV prefusion F vaccine effectiveness in older adults with immunosuppression: a prespecified analysis of the DAN-RSV trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Individuals with immunosuppression are at an increased risk of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a bivalent RSV prefusion F protein-based vaccine (RSVpreF) in older adults (≥60 years) according to immunosuppression status. METHODS: This study was a prespecified subgroup analysis of a pragmatic, open-label, nationwide randomised clinical trial conducted in Denmark during November-December, 2024. Older adults were randomised 1:1 to a single dose of RSVpreF or no vaccine. Immunosuppression was defined as at least one hospital encounter with an immunosuppressive condition or treatment. Baseline characteristics and outcomes were ascertained from nationwide registries. The primary outcome was hospitalisation for RSV-related respiratory tract disease, defined as respiratory hospitalisation with an RSV diagnosis code or a positive RSV test. Follow-up began 14 days after the scheduled study visit and continued until May 31, 2025. FINDINGS: Among the 131 276 participants (65 642 RSVpreF; 65 634 no vaccine), 5199 (4·0%) were immunosuppressed. In total, 21 participants were hospitalised with RSV-related respiratory tract disease, seven with immunosuppression, and 14 without immunosuppression. In the no-vaccine group, the incidence of RSV-related respiratory tract disease hospitalisation was more than nine-fold higher in participants with immunosuppression than in participants without (4·68 vs 0·50 events per 1000 person-years). As previously shown, RSVpreF significantly reduced RSV-related respiratory tract disease hospitalisations in the overall population (vaccine effectiveness 83·3% [95% CI 42·9 to 96·9]). No significant effect modification by immunosuppression status was observed (vaccine effectiveness 60·5% [95% CI -141·4 to 96·2] among those with immunosuppression and 92·3% [48·7 to 99·8] among those without immunosuppression; p for interaction=0·22). The point estimate was numerically lower among participants with immunosuppression, with a wide confidence interval crossing the null, but there was no statistical evidence of heterogeneity between subgroups. The estimated absolute rate reduction was 2·83 events per 1000 person-years (95% CI -2·00 to 7·66) among the participants with immunosuppression and 0·46 events per 1000 person-years (0·18 to 0·74) among those without immunosuppression. INTERPRETATION: In adults aged 60 years or older, RSVpreF vaccination reduced hospitalisations for RSV-related respiratory tract disease with no statistical evidence of effect modification by immunosuppression status; however, the study was not powered to exclude subgroup differences. Given the higher baseline risk of RSV-related hospitalisation observed among the individuals with immunosuppression, prioritising RSV vaccination in this group with high risk of severe RSV disease could have clinical benefits. The results of this trial could help to inform clinical guidance and vaccination policy, pending confirmation in larger studies. FUNDING: The DAN-RSV trial was supported by Pfizer.

title: Cohort trends in intrinsic capacity in Europe: a population-based longitudinal study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intrinsic capacity is a comprehensive measure of physical and mental capacities central to the WHO healthy ageing framework. Studies from England and China suggest that trajectories in intrinsic capacity are improving in more recently born older adults. However, whether similar improvements are occurring in other countries, in adults younger than 60 years, or across socioeconomic groups remains unknown. METHODS: We analysed seven waves (waves 1-2, 4-6, and 8-9) of The Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) between 2004 and 2022, including 80 105 adults aged 50 years or older in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. Intrinsic capacity was derived using confirmatory factor analysis across five subdomains (cognitive capacity, psychological capacity, sensory capacity, locomotor capacity, and vitality). Multilevel growth-curve models estimated associations of birth year with intrinsic capacity at first interview and within-person change over follow-up and variation by country, sex, and socioeconomic status (categorised as low, middle-low, middle-high, and high). We present model-based predictions for specific birth years (1920, 1930, 1940, 1950, and 1960), referred to here as birth cohorts. FINDINGS: The analytical sample of 80 105 respondents contributed 222 761 person-waves across the seven waves of SHARE. Across analytical person-waves, the mean age was 67·7 years (SD 10·3) and 43 289 (54·0%) of participants were women. More recently born participants had higher intrinsic capacity at study entry (birth year coefficient 0·797 [95% CI 0·780 to 0·815], p<0·0001) and slower 10-year rates of decline (linear change × birth year 0·426 [0·372 to 0·480], p<0·0001) than participants born earlier, although these gains in intrinsic capacity at study entry became progressively smaller (birth year squared -0·092 [-0·096 to -0·089], p<0·0001) and the slowing rate of decline weakened (linear change × birth year squared -0·047 [-0·059 to -0·036], p<0·0001) in more recently born participants. Similar trends were observed for each subdomain. Countries with lower intrinsic capacity levels in the 1920 birth cohort, such as Italy, showed larger gains in intrinsic capacity at study entry than countries with higher initial intrinsic capacity, such as Switzerland (eg, from the 1920 to the 1960 birth year cohorts: Italy, intrinsic capacity at study entry -1·880 [95% CI -1·953 to -1·808], p<0·0001, to 0·283 [0·246 to 0·319], p<0·0001; Switzerland, -0·705 [-0·775 to -0·636], p<0·0001, to 0·576 [0·541 to 0·611], p<0·0001) but smaller improvements in rates of decline (from the 1920 to the 1960 cohort: Italy, annual rate of decline in intrinsic capacity over 10 years -0·092 [95% CI -0·104 to -0·080], p<0·0001, to -0·011 [-0·017 to -0·006], p<0·0001; Switzerland, -0·121 [-0·132 to -0·111], p<0·0001, to -0·009 [-0·014 to -0·004], p=0·00040). Intrinsic capacity at study entry increased among more recently born participants of both the sexes, with women showing larger gains in intrinsic capacity than men (birth year coefficient: women 0·813 [0·789 to 0·837], p<0·0001; men 0·735 [0·708 to 0·762], p<0·0001), resulting in progressive narrowing of the sex-based difference in intrinsic capacity at study entry. Gains in intrinsic capacity at study entry across birth years were larger in higher socioeconomic status groups (birth year coefficient differences vs low socioeconomic status: middle-low 0·053 [95% CI 0·010 to 0·095], p=0·015; middle-high 0·100 [0·053 to 0·148], p<0·0001; and high 0·081 [0·031 to 0·131], p=0·0015), resulting in a widening of socioeconomic status differences across successive birth cohorts. INTERPRETATION: More recently born Europeans aged 50 years and older are in better health and show slower declines in intrinsic capacity compared with previous generations. However, these positive trends are unequally distributed and could be reaching a ceiling. Policy makers cannot assume that these trends will continue. The improving rates of decline in some countries underscore the value of continued investment in health care for older adults. FUNDING: Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Population Ageing Research and Velux Stiftung.

title: Healthy ageing for all? Socioeconomic inequalities in intrinsic capacity across generations
abstract: WHO defines healthy ageing as the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in older age.1 Functional ability encompasses the ability to meet basic needs, be mobile, learn, maintain relationships, and contribute to society. Within this framework, the functional ability of older adults is determined by their intrinsic capacity and environment. Intrinsic capacity is defined as all physical and mental capacities a person can draw upon and consists of five domains: vitality, locomotion, cognition, psychology, and sensory.

title: Making dementia clinical trials more representative
abstract: On Sept 21, 2026, Alzheimer's Disease International released its annual World Alzheimer Report. The theme of this year’s report is “A new era in dementia clinical trials” with a focus on examining the status of and demystifying clinical trials in the field. This focus is timely–as the report highlights, the number of drug development trials for Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias are increasing. This is in addition to an increasing number of non-pharmacological trials for dementia prevention and treatment.

title: Social connection and intrinsic capacity in later life across the USA, England, Europe, China, and Japan: a harmonised multicohort longitudinal study
abstract: Background Social connection represents a key modifiable determinant of healthy ageing, yet cross-national longitudinal evidence linking it to intrinsic capacity and its trajectories remains scarce. We examined whether baseline social connection was associated with baseline intrinsic capacity and annual intrinsic capacity change, whether associations differed across intrinsic capacity domains, and which components of social connection were most consistently associated with intrinsic capacity across cohorts. Methods The present study was a harmonised longitudinal cohort study using data from five ageing cohorts: the Health and Retirement Study (HRS; USA), English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA; England), Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE; Europe and Israel), China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; China), and Japanese Study of Aging and Retirement (JSTAR; Japan). Participants were aged 50 years or older. Baseline social connection was operationalised as a 0–5 composite score (marital or partnered status, living with others, family contact, friends or relatives contact, and social activity participation). Intrinsic capacity, encompassing locomotion, cognition, psychological, sensory, and vitality domains, was summed (0–10) and converted to cohort-specific and wave-specific Z scores. Survey-weighted linear mixed models with random intercepts estimated baseline associations adjusted for age, sex, educational attainment, household wealth tertile, and chronic disease burden. Trajectory models included time (years since baseline) and a social connection × time interaction. Cohort-specific estimates were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with false discovery rate (FDR) control for domain tests. Findings Among 39 021 participants (CHARLS 5538; ELSA 3294; HRS 3015; SHARE 26 239; and JSTAR 935), baseline age ranged from 61·1 in CHARLS to 70·8 years in HRS, the weighted proportion of males from 44·2% in HRS to 56·9% in JSTAR across cohorts, and follow-up ranged from two years in JSTAR to 12 years in ELSA. Higher baseline social connection was associated with higher total intrinsic capacity at baseline (pooled β=0·04 SD per 1-point increase; 95% CI 0·03–0·06). Domain-specific associations were the strongest for psychological (β=0·05 SD; 95% CI 0·03–0·06) and cognition (β=0·03 SD; 95% CI 0·01–0·05) domains, both remaining statistically significant after FDR correction. Locomotion showed a smaller association (β=0·02 SD; 95% CI 0·00–0·04) that remained significant after FDR correction. By contrast, sensory and vitality showed weaker associations that did not remain significant after FDR correction. Baseline social connection was not associated with differential rates of intrinsic capacity change over follow-up (pooled slope difference β=0·0024 SD per year; 95% CI −0·0004 to 0·0053; I 2 =26·3%). Among the five social connection components, social participation (β=0·13 SD; 95% CI 0·10–0·15) and married or partnered status (β=0·06 SD; 95% CI 0·02–0·09) showed the most consistent associations with higher total intrinsic capacity and remained statistically significant after FDR correction. Interpretation Across diverse cultural contexts, stronger social connection is consistently associated with higher baseline intrinsic capacity, particularly in cognitive and psychological domains. By contrast, we found no clear evidence that baseline social connection predicted differential rates of intrinsic capacity decline over follow-up. These findings support greater attention to social connection in healthy ageing policies and community services while recognising the need for further evidence on whether strengthening social connection can improve intrinsic capacity. Funding Department of Medicine & Therapeutics Geriatric Research Fund; CUHK Vice-Chancellor's Discretionary Fund.

title: Hearing loss, hearing-aid use, and mortality risk: individual participant data meta-analysis of population-based studies from Australia, Iceland, and the USA and a replication study from Norway
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hearing loss is associated with poorer health, depression, cognitive decline, and perhaps, with increased mortality risk. Whether hearing aids ameliorate this association is not well understood. We conducted a meta-analysis with a replication study to examine associations between hearing loss, current use of hearing aids, and mortality. METHODS: Hearing threshold data, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular disease (CVD)-related mortality (available across datasets) were analysed using individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis of three combined population-based studies: Blue Mountains Hearing Study (BMHS, Australia, 1997-2007), Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility-Reykjavik Study (AGES-RS, Iceland, 2002-06), and National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES, USA, 1999-2006). The Nord-Trøndelag Hearing Loss Study (NTHLS, Norway, 1996-98) was chosen for replication. An IPD meta-analysis of the combined consortium datasets for BMHS (n=2689), AGES-RS (n=5171), and NHANES (n=5992) was performed using Cox regression to estimate hazard ratios and 95% CIs, after adjusting for age, sex, education, BMI, smoking, angina or heart attack, diabetes, hypertension, stroke, and noise-exposure history; NTHLS data were analysed similarly. Hearing loss was defined by better ear pure-tone average categories endorsed by the Global Burden of Disease Hearing Loss Expert Group and WHO. FINDINGS: The IPD meta-analysis included 13 851 participants, with a mean age of 61·8 (SD 18·5; men 6228 [45·0%], women 7622 [55·0%]). Mild (1·19 [95% CI 1·10-1·29]), moderate (1·55 [1·42-1·70]), and moderately severe or worse (1·56 [1·38-1·76]) hearing loss were associated with increasing all-cause mortality risk. Mild (1·18 [95% CI 1·02-1·37]), moderate (1·43 [1·22-1·67]), and moderately severe or worse (1·30 [1·05-1·60]) hearing loss were also associated with increased CVD-related mortality risk. Current use of hearing aids was associated with reduced all-cause mortality risk [0·91 (95% CI 0·83-0·99)] and reduced CVD-related mortality [0·85 (0·73-0·99)]. The NTHLS replication study of 50 277 adults (men 23 532 [46·8%], women 26 745 [53·2%]) corroborated these findings. INTERPRETATION: The IPD meta-analysis and Norwegian NTHLS confirmed that increasing severity of hearing loss is significantly associated with higher mortality risk. Use of hearing aids was associated with reduced mortality risk. The potential link between hearing-aid use, other forms of hearing rehabilitation, and increased life expectancy in adults is an important area for future research investigation. FUNDING: Macquarie University; National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, National Institutes of Health; Icelandic Heart Association (Hjartavernd); National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; and Norwegian Institute of Public Health.

title: Hearing loss, hearing aids, and longevity: from association to intervention
abstract: Hearing loss is increasingly recognised as more than a disorder of communication. It is associated with cognitive decline, depression, social isolation, reduced physical functioning, and other adverse outcomes related to ageing. Whether hearing loss is also a marker—or potentially a contributor—to reduced longevity has attracted growing attention. In their Article published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, Chuan-Ming Li and colleagues address this question by presenting evidence from an individual participant data meta-analysis of population-based cohorts from Australia, Iceland, and the USA, complemented by replication in a Norwegian cohort.

title: Prevalence, management, and outcomes of urinary tract infections in older adults living in care homes versus older adults living outside care homes in the UK: a propensity score-matched case–control analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Globally, rising drug-resistant urinary tract infections (UTIs) affect older populations disproportionally. We aimed to assess the incidence, management, and patient outcomes of UTIs in English care homes. METHODS: Using linked primary, secondary, social care, and pathology data covering 2·5 million patients in London between 2018 and 2023, we matched older adults with UTIs living in care homes with older adults living outside care homes using propensity scores. We performed a time-series analysis of incidence and compared urine culture turnaround time and results (including antimicrobial resistance). We assessed UTI-related patient outcomes, including death, complications, recurrent infection, and antibiotic re-prescription within 60 days, using generalised estimating equations, adjusted for demographic and other risk factors. FINDINGS: We identified 91 501 UTI cases, including 6648 (7·3%) in care homes. In care homes, 4678 (70·4%) of the 6448 UTIs occurred in women and 3779 (56·8%) involved individuals aged 85 years or older. The older adults living in care homes were older (median age: 86 years [IQR 80-91] vs 76 years [71-83]) and more frequently White (70·3% vs 56·7%) than older adults living outside care homes. The incidence rate of community-acquired UTIs was 1909·4 per 100 000 person-months in care homes (increasing by 3·7 [95% CI 0·8-6·6] per month), as compared with 543·5 outside care homes (decreasing by 1·3 [-1·8 to -0·7] per month). Urine cultures were used less (1366 [20·5%] of 6648 [95% CI 19·6-21·5] vs 24 699 [29·1%] of 84 853 [28·8-29·4]), were more likely to be polymicrobial (suggesting contamination; 416 [30·4%] of 1366 [28·1-32·9] vs 4325 [17·5%] of 24 699 [17·0-18·0]), and had a longer turnaround time (52·9% turnaround in 1 day [50·3-55·6] vs 66·2% [65·6-66·8]) in care homes than outside care homes. Escherichia coli UTIs had higher resistance to trimethoprim (46·4% [95% CI 41·0-51·9] vs 32·0% [30·9-33·1]) and nitrofurantoin (7·5% [4·9-10·8] vs 2·4% [2·0-2·8]) in care homes than outside care homes. Care home cases had significantly worse 60-day outcomes, with higher risk of death (1·99 [95% CI 1·67-2·36]; p<0·001), presenting to general practitioners (1·38 [1·01-1·89]; p=0·042) and to hospitals (1·15 [1·01-1·32]; p=0·041) with complications, recurrent infections (1·22 [1·08-1·36]; p=0·001), and antibiotic re-prescription (1·11 [1·01-1·21]; p=0·024). INTERPRETATION: Older adults residing in care homes had higher UTI infection burden and worse clinical outcomes than matched older adults residing outside care homes. Possible explanatory factors include inadequate care, discordant prescribing decisions, and disconnect with diagnostic capabilities, in addition to the exacerbating effects on infection management during the COVID-19 pandemic. These findings highlight the need for improvement in infection management in care home settings. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research; Wellcome Trust; Fleming Initiative.

title: Highlights of EuGMS 2026
abstract: The theme for the 22nd European Geriatric Medicine Society (EuGMS) meeting, Sept 16–18, in Lille, France, was “Optimising Function: A Key to Healthy Ageing”. Accordingly, sessions centred around innovative approaches to improving geriatric healthcare, with the aim of protecting and promoting the independence and wellbeing of older adults.

title: The delirium we do not see
abstract: Hypoactive delirium is systematically under-recognised.1,2 Unlike hyperactive delirium, which often prompts immediate clinical attention, hypoactive delirium frequently goes unnoticed.1,2 Yet, hypoactive delirium accounts for an estimated 50–75% of delirium cases in hospitalised older adults aged 65 years and older and is associated with increased mortality and long-term cognitive and functional decline.1–3 Why the most common and one of the most serious presentations of delirium continues to be missed remains poorly understood.

title: Multimorbidity among older people in three African countries: a population-based cross-sectional study in The Gambia, South Africa, and Zimbabwe
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multimorbidity is intricately associated with global ageing and presents a key challenge for health systems and individuals. Despite growing recognition of this challenge, the gap in robust, comparable, population-level evidence on multimorbidity in Africa remains substantial. We aimed to describe multimorbidity among older people across five African sites in three countries representing different epidemiological and health-care contexts. METHODS: In this population-based cross-sectional study, we recruited adults aged at least 40 years in rural and urban The Gambia, rural and urban South Africa, and urban Zimbabwe (Feb 10, 2022 to Sept 2, 2024). Participants were stratified by site, age-band (40-54 years, 55-69 years, and ≥70 years), and sex. We included 5296 adults (median age 60 years, 53% were women) and recorded their self-reported medical conditions and current medications. We further assessed their height, weight, blood pressure, blood glucose, mental health symptoms, HIV status, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). We defined multimorbidity as having two or more of 26 chronic conditions. Multimorbidity prevalence was calculated weighted to each country's national population. We evaluated the risk factors for multimorbidity and associations of multimorbidity with HRQoL; multimorbidity clusters were described using latent class analysis. FINDINGS: 1926 (36%) of 5296 adults had multimorbidity. The weighted prevalence of multimorbidity was 36% (95% CI 35-37), ranging from 6·6% (5·1-8·1) in rural The Gambia to 62·0% (58·7-65·3) in urban South Africa. Across the three countries, education level, wealth, smoking, alcohol consumption, and BMI were the lowest in The Gambia and the greatest in South Africa, with a rural-urban gradient. Diabetes, hypertension, HIV, mood disorders, arthritis, and fragility fractures were the most common multimorbidity components. People with multimorbidity had lower HRQoL than those without multimorbidity. In Zimbabwe and South Africa, cardiometabolic (42-57% of the population) and HIV-related (25-48% of the population) multimorbidity clusters emerged, characterised by component diseases, risk factors, and associations with HRQoL. INTERPRETATION: Multimorbidity was found to be common among older people in five study settings in three African countries, with notable trends across sites. The high prevalence of multimorbidity in urban South Africa might foreshadow future trends across the African region as the continent's demographic and health transition advances, underscoring the urgent need for coordinated multisectoral strategies to address multimorbidity. FUNDING: Wellcome, National Institute for Health Research, and Medical Research Council.

title: Ageing in place: how to evaluate current practices following long-term care reforms
abstract: Governments worldwide are investing in ageing in place-that is, policies and programmes that enable older adults to remain in their homes and communities irrespective of income level or functional ability. However, there have been few concerted evaluation efforts to keep up with these reforms. Drawing on country examples from the Netherlands, Norway, and Japan, this Personal View identifies three recurring reform tensions: decentralisation versus coordination, personal versus collective responsibility, and cost containment versus investment. Each reform tension produces unintended consequences that evaluations can detect, prompting midcourse corrections. Importantly, existing evaluation frameworks remain narrowly focused on care expenditure, missing the wider societal consequences of reforms. These frameworks also overlook structural inequities that shape who can and cannot age in place with dignity. We therefore propose an integrated, equity-stratified framework to assess whether ageing in place reforms achieve their stated goals or instead widen the disparities they purport to address.

title: Overlooked and underserved: older adults in humanitarian contexts
abstract: Although not every older person is equally at risk, older people are among those most affected by humanitarian crises. Despite long-standing calls for more inclusive humanitarian action, older populations continue to be overlooked in preparedness, response, and recovery efforts. This Series paper critically examines the current policy landscape of humanitarian health care in relation to older populations and highlights a persistent gap between rhetoric and implementation. Additionally, factors contributing to the exclusion of older adults are documented, with factors operating at the institutional, interpersonal, and individual levels. These factors range from self-directed ageism and interpersonal neglect to systemic failures such as insufficient data, policy gaps, and service designs that fail to address the specific needs and rights of older adults. Drawing on available evidence, the paper also presents the severe consequences of the neglect of older populations, including avoidable deaths, worsening health outcomes, and increased care dependence. This Series paper calls for urgent action to ensure that older populations are meaningfully included in humanitarian action and serves as the foundation for the remaining papers in this Series.

title: PARTICIPATE: a rights-based framework to include older people’s health-care needs in humanitarian crises
abstract: The present paper concludes The Lancet Healthy Longevity Series on the health-care rights and needs of older people in humanitarian crises and outlines a rights-based framework for age-inclusive humanitarian public health approaches. The framework was shaped by an iterative process of consultation with key stakeholders and emphasises five fundamental rights that should guide humanitarian action. The fundamental rights include the rights to visibility and meaningful participation; non-discrimination; health; social care and protection from violence, exploitation, and neglect; and autonomy. We translate these fundamental rights into a concrete framework of actions, adopting the acronym PARTICIPATE, which aims to ensure inclusion and reduce excess mortality, morbidity, disability, exclusion, and care dependence among older people, while upholding their dignity, autonomy, and inherent worth in humanitarian crises. An accelerated commitment from humanitarian actors is urgently needed to meet the growing and diverse health-care rights and needs of older people, close gaps in health-care access, and embed accountability mechanisms for equitable, age-inclusive care. With consistent, rights-based engagement, genuine participation, and accountable systems, the humanitarian sector can uphold the rights and meet the health-care needs of older people, acknowledge their crucial roles and contributions, strengthen community resilience, and ensure justice across generations, thus remaining true to the core principles of humanitarian action.

title: Systematically overlooked: older adults in humanitarian emergencies
abstract: Across drought-affected rangelands, bombed cities, flooded plains, and refugee centres, older people live through crises that test not only their physical endurance but also their dignity. The experiences of older people in such settings reveal that they are disproportionately affected by emergencies yet consistently and systematically overlooked in response, a pattern well documented in humanitarian literature. Testimonies gathered through the community-based organisation networks of HelpAge International—from Kenya, Syria, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Ukraine, Gaza, South Sudan, and Venezuela—show how age is associated with disability, chronic illness, displacement, and poverty to create compounding, often life-threatening barriers to survival.

title: Malnutrition in humanitarian emergencies has no age limit
abstract: We welcome the opportunity to focus attention on the nutrition of a long neglected, yet highly vulnerable population group. Older adults (aged 60 years or older) are disproportionately affected by humanitarian emergencies. In these settings, malnutrition among older adults is often hidden in plain sight—overshadowed by chronic disease, mistaken for normal ageing—and its effects on health, wellbeing, and independence are underestimated.

title: The invisible gap: sexual and reproductive health and rights for older people in humanitarian emergencies
abstract: By 2050, more than one in five people will be considered older persons, aged 60 years or older, accounting for more than 2·1 billion people.1 Simultaneous to this demographic evolution is the intensification of sudden-onset and protracted humanitarian crises. Despite these parallel trends, older people are often overlooked within the humanitarian architecture, even as their needs become compounded by disability, cognitive decline, limited mobility, and other comorbidities that have accumulated and compounded across the life course.

title: Addressing the health rights and needs of older adults in humanitarian contexts: the importance of person-centred approaches
abstract: Humanitarian health responses often fall short in delivering inclusive assistance that upholds the rights of older people and meets their health needs. Here, we define older people as those who self-identify or are recognised as such within their specific social and cultural contexts, which allows us to account for different life expectancies and changes in social roles across settings. At the same time that responses fall short, environmental disasters, armed conflict, disease outbreaks, displacement, and the effects of the climate emergency often disproportionately affect older adults. Consequently, a substantial and growing proportion of the older population is excluded from humanitarian health assistance and experience poor health outcomes. This Series paper adopted a multimethod approach that combined existing evidence syntheses, an additional literature review, an expert consultation, and case studies from health programmes in Afghanistan and Gaza, occupied Palestine, to examine the health needs and rights of older people in contexts affected by humanitarian crises. Using an ecosystem of determinants approach, this Series paper highlights how factors across humanitarian crisis contexts-including rights, equity, and inclusion; enabling environments and relationships; and essential needs and supports-interact to shape physical and cognitive health, functional ability, mental wellbeing, values, lived experiences, priorities, and preferences among older people. The Series paper further explores the complexity of older people's health needs, including the impacts of multimorbidity, frailty, and polypharmacy, and examines the importance of person-centred care approaches that respond to individual circumstances and priorities. Additionally, the Series paper explores person-centred care as a pathway to advancing health equity and upholding the rights of older people and examines barriers to implementing person-centred care approaches in contemporary humanitarian responses.

title: Palliative care as a fundamental right for older adults in humanitarian crises: closing a persistent inequity gap
abstract: Older adults remain among the most invisible populations in humanitarian crises. Evidence from The Lancet Healthy Longevity Series shows that their health, functional, and psychosocial needs are frequently overlooked, driven by misconceptions about ageing and age-related bias in emergency planning and response, and compounded by intersectional vulnerabilities such as gender, disability, displacement, and poverty.1 Humanitarian responses often adopt disease-focused, survival-driven models that inadequately address older adults’ complex, person-centred and community-centred needs, and their voices are further marginalised through exclusion from policy processes.

title: Statin discontinuation in older adults: does frailty matter?

Efficacy and safety of statin discontinuation in patients 65 years and older according to frailty status: a population-wide retrospective cohort study in England using Clinical Practice Research Datalink data
abstract: BACKGROUND: In older patients (≥65 years), the evidence for continued statin prescription is scarce. Although statins are commonly discontinued in the context of advancing age or frailty, there is little evidence to guide decision making. Hence, we aimed to investigate the risks and benefits of statin discontinuation in older people, stratified by frailty status. METHODS: In this English population-wide retrospective cohort study, we used Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD data of routinely collected and anonymised patient records. Eligible patients were registered at a general practice providing research-quality data between Jan 1, 1998, and May 20, 2021. The inclusion criteria were persistent statin users (defined as a statin medication possession ratio of 80% or more for any statin during the preceding 12 months before study entry) aged 65 years or older and Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) and Office for National Statistics linkage availability. Eligible patients were persistent statin users registered with an up-to-standard practice contributing to CPRD GOLD. Statin discontinuation was defined as no new prescription in the 180 days after the last prescription expired. Participants who discontinued statins were matched within the practice to two randomly selected statin continuers, who were actively taking statins on the discontinuation date. The primary outcome measure was all-cause hospitalisation, defined as a new admission date in HES with discharge data after at least 24 h of admission, measured at 1 year and 5 years of the index date. The effect of statin discontinuation was examined using Fine-Gray models accounting for the competing risk of death. Results were stratified by electronic frailty index category (fit, mild frailty, moderate frailty, and severe frailty), dementia, care home residency, or housebound status in the preceding year. RESULTS: We identified 383 342 eligible persistent stain users, of whom 65 727 participants discontinued statins and were matched with 131 453 participants who continued statins (mean age 75·9 years [SD 7·2], 98 378 [49.9%] female and 65 727 [50.1%] male) over a mean follow-up period of 4·1 years (SD 3·3). After Inverse probability of treatment weighting, there were 136 100 participants who continued a statin and 61 080 who discontinued. There were 94 725 hospital admissions over 551 178 person-years, with crude incidence rates of 199·7 per 1000 person-years (95% CI 197·5-201·9) in those who discontinued statin therapy and 160·2 per 1000 person-years (158·9-161·5) in those who continued statin therapy. Discontinuation was associated with an increased relative risk of all-cause hospitalisation at 1 year in the whole cohort (subdistribution hazard ratio [sHR] 1·22 [95% CI 1·20-1·25]; absolute risk difference [ARD] per 1000 patients 37·6 [95% CI 33.7-41.4]). The relative risk reduced with increasing frailty (fit sHR 1·30 [95% CI 1·24-1·37], ARD per 1000 patients 30·2 [95% CI 24·7-35·8]; mild frailty sHR 1·22 [1·18-1·26], ARD per 1000 patients 38·5 [32·1-45·6]; and moderate frailty sHR 1·16 [1·10-1·21], ARD per 1000 patients 40·0 [28·2-53·4]), and there was no association between statin discontinuation and an increased risk of all-cause hospitalisation among patients with severe frailty (sHR 1·03 [0·94-1·12], ARD per 1000 patients 9·0 [-19·9 to 34·8]) or dementia (sHR 1·05 [0·99-1·12], ARD per 1000 patients 13·6 [-0·4 to 33·4]), and among care home residents (sHR 0·76 [0·63-0·90], ARD per 1000 patients -68·8 [-112·8 to -27·0]); a small increased risk was observed among those who were housebound (sHR 1·07 [1·02-1·12], ARD per 1000 patients 20·8 [5·5-35·1]). At 5 years, statin discontinuation was associated with an increased relative risk of all-cause hospitalisation in the whole cohort (sHR 1·11 [95% CI 1·09-1·12]; ARD per 1000 patients 36·9 [31·5-41·5]). Again, this risk reduced with increasing frailty (fit sHR 1·14 [95% CI 1·11-1·17], ARD per 1000 patients 41·1 [95% CI 32·3-50·4]; mild frailty sHR 1·11 [1·08-1·13], ARD per 1000 patients 37·4 [29·4-45·9]; and moderate frailty sHR 1·04 [1·01-1·08], ARD per 1000 patients 15·2 [5·9-27·7]), and there was no association between statin discontinuation and an increased risk of all-cause hospitalisation among participants with severe frailty (sHR 0·94 [0·88-1·00], ARD per 1000 patients -19·7 [-40·9 to -2·0]) or dementia (sHR 0·95 [0·91-0·99], ARD per 1000 patients -20·2 [-38·5 to -0·3]), among care home residents (sHR 0·71 [0·62-0·81], ARD per 1000 patients -120·4 [-173·0 to -70·3]), and in those who were housebound (sHR 0·96 [0·93-1·00], ARD per 1000 patients -12·5 [-25·6 to 1·1]). INTERPRETATION: In older adults, statin discontinuation was associated with an increased risk of hospitalisation, although this association diminished with increasing frailty. These findings could inform individualised deprescribing decisions, although residual confounding can hinder causal interpretation. FUNDING: National Institute of Health Research and Wellcome Trust.

title: Frailty as a determinant of mRNA vaccine efficacy
abstract: Frailty, an age-related state of increased vulnerability, is associated with greater susceptibility to infection and impaired vaccine response. In this Review, we examine how frailty-associated immunosenescence, including altered haematopoiesis, chronic inflammation, and dysfunction of innate and adaptive immune responses, can affect the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines. Evidence from COVID-19 lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines and other vaccines suggests that people living with frailty can mount weaker or less durable responses than non-frail peers, although findings remain heterogeneous and frailty-specific evidence is scarce. The high customisability of lipid nanoparticle mRNA platforms creates opportunities for frailty-tailored vaccination. We discuss optimisation of lipid nanoparticle composition, targeting and dosing, mRNA cargo and combination-vaccine approaches, alongside host-directed measures addressing comorbidities, nutrition, and immune dysfunction. Integrating frailty into vaccine design, evaluation, and deployment could support safer, more effective, and more individualised vaccination strategies for older adults.

title: Upholding the rights of older adults in humanitarian crises
abstract: Humanitarian crises, including armed conflict, natural disasters, or displacement, threaten the rights, safety, and health of people worldwide. According to data from the Disaster Risk Management Knowledge Centre, the average global risk of humanitarian crises has increased over the past decade, with low-income and middle-income countries carrying the largest burden. In addition, older adults are disproportionately affected by humanitarian crises and are frequently overlooked, meaning that their basic needs are often unmet.

title: Estimating the population-level non-respiratory burden of severe influenza: a systematic review of methods and estimates
abstract: Influenza is widely recognised as a respiratory infection, although the condition can also exacerbate or trigger serious non-respiratory outcomes that are often overlooked in burden assessments. Previous reviews have separately evaluated how methodological choices affect influenza-associated mortality and hospitalisation estimates and have covered non-respiratory outcomes in part, although these studies were restricted to select causes or severe outcomes, specific populations, or particular geographical settings. A more comprehensive synthesis focused specifically on severe non-respiratory influenza burden has been missing. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review of 238 studies from 52 countries or regions examining both the burden of severe influenza beyond respiratory disease and the estimation methods used. We found that non-respiratory outcomes represent a substantial component of the total influenza burden, with a pronounced age gradient disproportionately affecting older adults (≥65 years). Cardiovascular events were particularly notable, contributing to more than 50 deaths and 60 hospitalisations per 100 000 older adults. Burden estimates also varied by analytical method, cause, and study period, and most evidence was concentrated in high-income settings, leaving important geographical gaps. Our findings highlight that influenza burden assessments and prevention strategies should extend beyond respiratory presentations, particularly for older populations, and emphasise upon the need for standardised methods and broader geographical coverage to generate estimates that are more comparable across studies and settings that better inform public health policy and resource allocation.
